title: N5 Biology Experimental Skills Lab
basis: Original practice questions informed by 2026–27 course specification and official 2025 report; not reproduced past-paper questions.

skills.title: Writing aims
skills.subtitle: State what changes and what is measured.

skills.title: Identifying variables
skills.subtitle: Separate independent, dependent and controlled variables.

skills.title: Using controls
skills.subtitle: Choose a meaningful comparison without treatment.

skills.title: Validity
skills.subtitle: Spot factors that could make a test unfair.

skills.title: Presenting data
skills.subtitle: Choose graphs, scales, labels and sensible tables.

skills.title: Drawing conclusions
skills.subtitle: Use evidence to answer the aim—not just list results.

skills.title: Evaluating methods
skills.subtitle: Suggest specific changes that improve an investigation.

skills.title: Fieldwork skills
skills.subtitle: Practise quadrats, transects, pitfall traps and sampling.

skills.title: Scientific evidence
skills.subtitle: Decide what data can and cannot show.

questions.stem: A class changes water-bath temperature and measures how much oxygen catalase produces in one minute. Which is the clearest aim?
options: To investigate catalase and oxygen.
To find the best temperature for enzymes.
To investigate the effect of temperature on the volume of oxygen produced by catalase in one minute.
To investigate the effect of oxygen on water temperature.
questions.explanation: The aim names the independent variable (temperature) and the dependent measurement (volume of oxygen in a fixed time).
questions.hint: Find the option naming both what is changed and what is measured.
questions.pitfall: The other aims are vague, reverse the variables or fail to say what was measured.

questions.stem: Pupils place equal-size quadrats at different distances from a footpath and count daisies. Which aim matches the method?
options: To investigate how distance from a footpath affects the number of daisies per quadrat.
To investigate which flower is the prettiest near a path.
To investigate whether daisies like paths.
To measure the distance along a path.
questions.explanation: The aim links distance from the path (independent variable) to daisy count in equal-area quadrats (dependent variable).
questions.hint: Think about the quantity deliberately varied and the quantity counted.

questions.stem: A learner puts identical potato cylinders in different salt concentrations and records percentage change in mass. Choose the most precise aim.
options: To see what happens to potatoes.
To investigate how different potatoes affect salt concentration.
To measure mass using a balance.
To investigate the effect of salt concentration on the percentage change in potato mass.
questions.explanation: Salt concentration is changed; percentage change in mass is measured. The specific measurement matters.
questions.hint: An aim should not be just a method or equipment list.

questions.stem: A student varies the distance of a lamp from pondweed and counts oxygen bubbles each minute. Which aim fits the actual method?
options: To prove light causes photosynthesis.
To investigate the effect of distance from a lamp on the number of bubbles produced per minute by pondweed.
To investigate the effect of oxygen bubbles on the distance from a lamp.
To investigate pondweed growth after a month.
questions.explanation: The chosen aim specifies lamp distance and bubble count per minute; the method does not directly measure light intensity or growth.
questions.hint: Describe what is actually changed, not just the process you hope it represents.

questions.stem: A student adds 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8 g of fertiliser to identical pots, then measures mean plant height after 21 days. Best aim?
options: To prove fertiliser improves all plant growth.
To see whether fertiliser is good.
To investigate how mass of fertiliser affects mean plant height after 21 days.
To compare plant species in different fields.
questions.explanation: The aim accurately names fertiliser mass and mean height after a set interval without presuming the outcome.
questions.hint: Avoid an aim that already states the result.

questions.stem: An investigation changes wind speed and records how much mass a leafy shoot loses in 20 minutes. Which aim is assessable?
options: To investigate the effect of wind speed on mass lost by a leafy shoot in 20 minutes.
To compare how much water is in different winds.
To increase water loss in plants.
To examine the movement of all substances through stems.
questions.explanation: The changed variable and measurable outcome are both clear.
questions.hint: Pick the one whose variables match the equipment and measurements.

questions.stem: Equal discs soaked in different plant extracts are placed on a bacterial lawn; clear-zone diameter is measured. Which aim is appropriate?
options: To prove plant extracts kill all bacteria.
To identify which plant is safest to eat.
To study bacteria in general.
To investigate the effect of extract type on the diameter of the clear zone around each disc.
questions.explanation: This describes what can actually be measured rather than claiming all bacteria were killed.
questions.hint: Distinguish a measured observation from an untested claim.

questions.stem: A pupil tests the effect of pH on amylase and also tries to measure how temperature affects germination in the same investigation. Why might the suggested combined aim be weak?
options: Every aim must include the name of an organism.
It combines two separate independent variables and two different dependent variables.
Aims must start with the word “prove”.
Aims should list every item of apparatus.
questions.explanation: A focused investigation has a clearly identifiable question; mixing unrelated changes and measurements makes the conclusion harder to link to the aim.
questions.hint: Consider whether one set of measurements could answer the whole aim.

questions.stem: A student changes wind speed but keeps light intensity and leaf area the same. What is the independent variable?
options: Water lost
Leaf area
Wind speed
Light intensity
questions.explanation: Wind speed is deliberately varied. Water lost is the measured response.
questions.hint: Identify what the student deliberately changes.

questions.stem: The mass of fertiliser is changed and mean seedling height is measured after 21 days. What is the dependent variable?
options: Mean seedling height
Mass of fertiliser
Time at measurement
Volume of soil
questions.explanation: Mean seedling height is the quantity recorded to see the effect of fertiliser.
questions.hint: The dependent variable is the outcome recorded.

questions.stem: Temperature is varied and oxygen volume in one minute is measured. Which pair of variables should be kept constant?
options: Temperature and oxygen volume
Type of catalase and hydrogen peroxide concentration
Temperature and rate of oxygen production
Oxygen volume and reaction rate
questions.explanation: Using the same enzyme source and substrate concentration helps isolate temperature as the cause.
questions.hint: Choose two factors that could otherwise change the reaction and are not the variables being investigated.

questions.stem: Potato cylinders are placed in various salt concentrations. Which is a sensible controlled variable?
options: Percentage mass change
Salt concentration
Final mass after soaking
Length and diameter of potato cylinders
questions.explanation: Equal-sized cylinders help ensure comparable results; salt concentration must change.
questions.hint: Look for something kept the same in every group.

questions.stem: Lamp distance is changed and pondweed bubbles per minute are counted. What is the dependent variable?
options: Distance from lamp
Type of bulb
Number of bubbles per minute
Duration of the investigation
questions.explanation: Bubbles per minute are counted as the outcome when lamp distance changes.
questions.hint: Ask which measurement provides the results.

questions.stem: A pupil measures heart rate before exercise and after 1, 2 and 3 minutes of exercise. Which is the independent variable?
options: Heart rate
Exercise duration
Number of heartbeats
Heart-rate increase
questions.explanation: Exercise duration is deliberately varied; heart rate is measured.
questions.hint: Which condition is set to different values?

questions.stem: Quadrats of the same area are placed 1–5 m from a path. Which pair correctly identifies the independent and dependent variables?
options: Daisy count; distance
Quadrat area; distance
Distance; quadrat area
Distance; daisy count
questions.explanation: Distance from the path is varied and the number of daisies counted. Quadrat area is held constant.
questions.hint: Look at the order: changed variable first, measured outcome second.

questions.stem: Two groups compare plant growth under different colours of light. One group waters its plants twice as often. What else now varies?
options: The amount of water supplied
The colour of light only
The way height is measured only
The species of plant, necessarily
questions.explanation: Water availability varies alongside light colour, introducing another possible cause of any difference.
questions.hint: Look for a condition that should not change between groups.

questions.stem: Yeast is given different sugar concentrations and gas production is recorded. What is the purpose of a 0% sugar set-up?
options: To increase the rate of respiration
To act as a comparison with no added sugar
To ensure the gas volume is high
To increase the number of repeats
questions.explanation: A set-up with no added sugar provides a comparison when the treatment is absent.
questions.hint: Think about what the 0% condition adds to the comparison.

questions.stem: A student tests whether a plant extract inhibits bacterial growth using paper discs. Which control is most suitable?
options: A larger disc soaked in a concentrated extract
A disc with a different unknown extract
A disc soaked in the solvent only
A disc placed on a different species of bacteria
questions.explanation: A solvent-only disc tests whether the solvent or paper itself causes a clear zone.
questions.hint: The control should omit the tested extract while leaving the other conditions comparable.

questions.stem: A plant leaf is placed in a container with carbon dioxide available. Which comparison best tests the effect of removing carbon dioxide?
options: An identical leaf in the same conditions but with carbon dioxide absorbed
Another species of plant in bright light
The same leaf after several weeks of growth
An identical leaf at a different temperature
questions.explanation: The comparison varies carbon dioxide availability while other conditions stay the same.
questions.hint: Aim for only one meaningful difference between the two set-ups.

questions.stem: A pupil tests active amylase on starch and measures a clear zone. Which comparison best checks whether the enzyme is necessary?
options: Use a stronger starch concentration and active enzyme
Use active enzyme at two temperatures
Use twice as much active enzyme
Use boiled amylase instead of active amylase while keeping other conditions constant
questions.explanation: The boiled-enzyme comparison removes active enzyme activity while keeping the basic set-up similar.
questions.hint: Think of how to remove or inactivate the treatment of interest.

questions.stem: Leafy shoots lose mass in a wind experiment. Which set-up could help identify mass loss not caused by leaves?
options: A larger leafy shoot in stronger wind
An otherwise similar set-up without leaves
A shoot with extra leaves in a sealed container
The same shoot with a different balance
questions.explanation: A comparison without leaves gives a baseline for mass changes from the apparatus or other tissue.
questions.hint: A control removes the component whose role is being tested.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the role of a control in an experiment?
options: A set-up used to compare results when the treatment is not applied
A repeat of a treatment to calculate an average
The variable the researcher measures
A promise that all measurements are accurate
questions.explanation: A control provides a comparison when the treatment is absent; it is not simply another repeat.
questions.hint: A control is a comparison, rather than a mathematical calculation.

questions.stem: A student compares how different quantities of fertiliser affect seedlings. What is a suitable control?
options: A pot given 8 g of fertiliser
A pot containing a different plant species
An otherwise identical pot given no fertiliser
A pot kept in darkness
questions.explanation: The no-fertiliser pot is the untreated comparison; conditions such as species and light should match.
questions.hint: Choose the untreated group, not a group with several changes.

questions.stem: A test changes the temperature but also uses a different concentration of hydrogen peroxide each time. What is the main problem?
options: The experiment has too many repeats
The dependent variable is being measured
The investigation becomes more reliable
The investigation is less valid because two factors could affect oxygen production
questions.explanation: Substrate concentration is another possible cause of changed oxygen output, so temperature is not isolated.
questions.hint: Ask whether the measured effect can be attributed to the intended changed variable.

questions.stem: A student tests the effect of fertiliser on height, but different groups get different amounts of water. Which term best describes the problem?
options: Validity
Reliability only
Accuracy of the ruler only
Graph scale
questions.explanation: Water is a confounding variable; validity is weakened because observed differences may not be due to fertiliser.
questions.hint: Think about whether another variable could explain the effect.

questions.stem: Seedlings in light are compared with seedlings in darkness. The light group is at 25°C and the dark group at 15°C. Which improvement best increases validity?
options: Repeat both groups with the same temperature
Use taller seedlings only in the light group
Record height less frequently
Add an unrelated third plant species
questions.explanation: Controlling temperature makes it more likely that differences result from light rather than temperature.
questions.hint: Keep every other influential condition alike.

questions.stem: A pupil compares insect numbers in grass and woodland. Traps in grass are left for 2 hours, traps in woodland for 24 hours. Why is the comparison weak?
options: Insects are always absent from grass
Longer exposure can alter how many are caught independent of habitat
Pitfall traps cannot sample invertebrates
Repeating the investigation would automatically remove the difference in duration
questions.explanation: Different sampling durations are a confounding factor, so habitat is not isolated.
questions.hint: Look for unequal sampling effort.

questions.stem: Some potato cylinders are twice as thick as others when salt concentration is tested. Which change makes the test more valid?
options: Use a larger range of salt concentrations only
Use a thermometer rather than a balance
Use cylinders of the same dimensions
Take the mean of two unequal cylinders
questions.explanation: Matching cylinder dimensions controls surface area and mass differences that could alter the outcome.
questions.hint: Isolate salt concentration by standardising the sample size.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes experimental validity in National 5 Biology?
options: Taking as many photographs as possible
Obtaining identical results in repeated trials
Using a large number of different independent variables
Controlling other variables so an effect is likely to be due to the variable changed
questions.explanation: Validity concerns whether the effect can reasonably be linked to the variable being investigated.
questions.hint: Validity asks: was it a fair investigation of that variable?

questions.stem: A study compares daisy numbers 1–5 m from a path but uses 1 m² quadrats near the path and 0.25 m² quadrats farther away. What should change?
options: Use quadrats of equal area at every distance
Count a different plant near the path
Place all quadrats at 1 m
Change the field site after each count
questions.explanation: Different quadrat areas create an unfair comparison of raw counts. Equal area allows better comparison.
questions.hint: Look at sampling effort and area, not just where the counts were taken.

questions.stem: A study compares heart rate before and after exercise. Some participants drink caffeine and others do not. What conclusion is best?
options: Caffeine proves exercise never affects heart rate
Caffeine may influence heart rate, weakening validity unless controlled
More participants would guarantee caffeine has no effect
Using the same stopwatch is the only necessary control
questions.explanation: Caffeine is another factor that may affect heart rate; it should be controlled or accounted for.
questions.hint: Identify other factors affecting the recorded outcome.

questions.stem: Repeated plant heights for one treatment are 8.1, 8.0, 13.4 and 8.2 cm. Which observation needs checking?
options: 8.0 cm
8.1 cm
8.2 cm
questions.explanation: 13.4 cm is far from the other readings and may be anomalous; investigate before deciding what to do with it.
questions.hint: Look for the value that is inconsistent with the others.

questions.stem: Which set of repeated oxygen readings is most consistent?
questions.explanation: The second set varies by just 1 cm³, indicating good consistency between repeats.
questions.hint: Reliability is about how similar repeated readings are.

questions.stem: A student obtains one oxygen-volume measurement at every temperature. What would best improve reliability?
options: Use a completely different reaction at each temperature
Change the concentration every time
Replace the independent variable
Repeat at every temperature and examine whether values are consistent
questions.explanation: Repeating each condition allows consistency and anomalies to be assessed.
questions.hint: More repetitions under the same conditions are helpful.

questions.stem: A fair investigation is repeated three times at each temperature but gives very different readings each time. Which statement is justified?
options: The repeated results are not very reliable
Controlling variables guarantees reliable results
Different results prove that temperature has no effect
Repeats always make the original results more valid
questions.explanation: Validity and reliability are different; large disagreement between repeats suggests poor reliability even when variables are controlled.
questions.hint: Consider consistency rather than whether the experiment is fair.

questions.stem: Four repeats give 8.1, 8.0, 13.4 and 8.2 cm. What is the best next step?
options: Always delete 13.4 without comment
Change 13.4 to 8.4 to fit the pattern
Check the recorded value and method, and repeat if appropriate
Report only the highest value
questions.explanation: An unusual measurement should be investigated, not silently removed or altered.
questions.hint: Scientists should not change recorded data to fit an expected pattern.

questions.stem: Two treatments have repeats of A: 12, 11, 13 and B: 20, 19, 21. What do the repeats show?
options: Both treatments have identical results
Within each treatment the values are quite consistent
Treatment B proves the result will be identical for any species
The experiment is invalid because the measurements differ slightly
questions.explanation: Each treatment gives a narrow spread of values, indicating consistent results for those repeats.
questions.hint: Small differences among repeats are normal; assess their spread.

questions.stem: A field study uses one pitfall trap for one afternoon. Which change is most likely to improve reliability?
options: Change the habitat every hour
Use a trap without recording its location
Count only the largest animal
Use multiple comparable traps and repeat sampling
questions.explanation: Replicate traps and repeat visits help identify whether counts are consistent instead of relying on one observation.
questions.hint: Consider increasing the number of comparable observations.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes reliability from validity?
options: Reliability concerns consistency in repeats; validity concerns controlling other variables
Reliability concerns how fair the test is; validity is only its sample size
Reliability is the size of the measured effect; validity is whether graph axes are labelled
Both words mean exactly the same thing
questions.explanation: The course specification explicitly separates consistent repeated results from controlling other variables.
questions.hint: One term relates to repeats; the other to isolating the cause.

questions.stem: When graphing temperature against oxygen volume, which is the most appropriate horizontal axis?
options: Volume of oxygen (cm³)
Time taken to clean glassware (s)
Temperature (°C)
Number of enzyme molecules
questions.explanation: The independent variable, temperature, belongs on the x-axis and needs its unit.
questions.hint: The independent variable normally goes along the horizontal axis.

questions.stem: A pupil measures oxygen produced at temperatures of 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50°C. Which graph is most suitable for displaying the relationship?
options: Line graph or plotted points joined to show the continuous relationship
Pie chart of oxygen volume by month
A bar chart with no numerical scale
A pictogram showing different enzymes
questions.explanation: Temperature is continuous, so an x–y graph is suitable for showing the relationship.
questions.hint: Think whether the independent variable is numerical and continuous.

questions.stem: A class compares numbers of woodlice caught at three named sites: garden, playground and woodland. Which graph is usually most suitable?
options: Line graph treating sites as continuous numbers
Pie chart that must total 100%
Scattergraph of temperature only
Bar chart with each site as a category
questions.explanation: Named sampling sites are separate categories, so a bar chart is a clear display.
questions.hint: Ask whether the independent variable consists of named categories.

questions.stem: A student records reaction time in seconds at different temperatures in °C. Which pair of table headings is clear?
options: Temperature | Reaction
Temperature (°C) | Reaction time (s)
Temperature in seconds | Reaction time in °C
Trial | Numbers
questions.explanation: Both headings name the quantity and give the relevant units.
questions.hint: Include the measured quantity and unit in each numerical heading.

questions.stem: A graph plots lamp distance (cm) against bubbles per minute. Which y-axis label is correct?
options: Distance (cm)
Photosynthesis
Number of bubbles per minute
Light (minutes)
questions.explanation: Bubble production per minute is the dependent measurement and belongs on the vertical axis.
questions.hint: The vertical axis should identify what was measured, with appropriate units.

questions.stem: Look at the graph of lamp distance and bubble production. What happens to bubble count as the lamp moves from 10 to 40 cm?
options: It decreases from about 28 to 5 per minute
It rises from about 5 to 28 per minute
It stays at 28 per minute
The graph contains no information about bubble count
questions.explanation: The plotted points show fewer bubbles counted per minute at greater distances from the lamp.
questions.hint: Read values at the first and last x-axis positions.

questions.stem: A class plots plant heights between 0 and 16 cm. Which vertical axis scale is easiest to use accurately?
options: 0, 3, 7, 11, 16 at equally spaced grid lines
0, 1, 4, 9, 16 at equally spaced grid lines
16, 14, 12, 10, 8 with no units
0, 4, 8, 12, 16 at equally spaced grid lines
questions.explanation: Equal grid distances must represent equal numerical intervals on a linear scale.
questions.hint: Check the difference between consecutive labels.

questions.stem: At each temperature pupils measure gas volume three times. Which table layout helps compare results and calculate a mean?
options: Temperature, a single unexplained number
Temperature, repeat 1, repeat 2, repeat 3, mean (with units)
Only the final mean and no temperature values
A list of times when pupils used the equipment
questions.explanation: Showing each repeat and the mean under clear headings makes the data transparent and allows consistency to be checked.
questions.hint: Keep the independent variable and each measurement visible.

questions.stem: Use the graph. Which conclusion is supported by the fertiliser results?
options: Fertiliser always makes plants taller at any amount
The best growth occurs at precisely 5 g
Mean height increases up to 4 g, levels off at 6 g, then decreases at 8 g
All plants died when 8 g was applied
questions.explanation: The graph shows 6, 10, 14, 14 and 11 cm as fertiliser mass increases; the conclusion follows the entire pattern.
questions.hint: Check whether the statement accounts for every data point, including the downturn.
questions.pitfall: Avoid extrapolating beyond the tested values or ignoring parts of the trend.

questions.stem: Use the table. Which conclusion is the most defensible?
options: Catalase produces the greatest measured oxygen volume at 30°C among the tested temperatures
Catalase is completely inactive above 50°C
Catalase always works best at 37°C
Temperature has no effect on gas production
questions.explanation: Of the temperatures shown, 30°C gives the highest measured volume, 13 cm³. Nothing here establishes behaviour outside the tested range.
questions.hint: Make a claim limited to the actual measurements.

questions.stem: Use the data. What conclusion best relates to the investigation of salt concentration and percentage change in potato mass?
options: Potatoes cannot take in water
Higher salt concentration was associated with a lower percentage change in mass, from +14% at 0% to −8% at 6%
All potatoes lose the same percentage mass
The balance must have been broken
questions.explanation: The recorded mass changes become progressively lower as salt concentration rises, with a switch from gain to loss.
questions.hint: Describe the overall trend, including the direction of change.

questions.stem: The table shows wind speed and mass lost by a shoot. Which conclusion answers the aim?
options: The wind speeds tested were 0, 1, 2 and 3 m/s
The heaviest shoot was 2.1 g
Wind makes plants stronger
Over the tested range, increasing wind speed was associated with increased mass loss
questions.explanation: Mass loss rises from 0.4 to 2.1 g as wind speed rises from 0 to 3 m/s; the claim directly connects the variables.
questions.hint: A conclusion connects the changed variable to the measured response.

questions.stem: Use the table. Which conclusion is supported by the results?
options: Sugar concentration had no effect
8% sugar caused no gas production
Gas production increased to 6% sugar then was slightly lower at 8%
Higher sugar concentration always gives a higher gas volume
questions.explanation: Gas volume increases from 0 to 28 cm³ at 6%, then falls slightly to 27 cm³ at 8%.
questions.hint: Check for a peak or reversal instead of assuming a straight-line trend.

questions.stem: Use the quadrat results. Which conclusion is best?
options: Daisy count increased with distance from the path over the 1–5 m range
All flowers grow better away from every path
Daisies completely avoid the footpath
The daisy count was always 10
questions.explanation: The number increases from 2 daisies at 1 m to 10 at 5 m; that is the pattern measured here.
questions.hint: Stay within the studied distances and species.

questions.stem: What makes a scientific conclusion stronger than merely restating the results?
options: Repeating all the raw numbers without interpretation
Making a claim about the relationship investigated, supported by the evidence
Adding personal opinions about what should have happened
Ignoring results that differ from the prediction
questions.explanation: The conclusion answers the aim and interprets the trend using evidence, rather than simply listing observations.
questions.hint: Think about the difference between describing values and answering the question investigated.

questions.stem: Plants were taller with 4 g fertiliser than with 0 g, but height fell at 8 g. Which conclusion avoids an overclaim?
options: Every extra gram of fertiliser causes more growth
Fertiliser has no effect on height
The trial proves plants are poisoned above 4 g
Moderate fertiliser amounts increased mean height, but the largest tested amount reduced it compared with 4–6 g
questions.explanation: The conclusion recognises the increase and decline without claiming a mechanism that was not tested.
questions.hint: Your conclusion should cover increases and decreases in the results.

questions.stem: A school survey finds pupils who sleep more hours tend to score higher in tests. Which conclusion is justified?
options: Extra sleep alone has been proved to cause better marks
The survey measured students’ brain cells
The data show an association, but other factors might also affect scores
Every pupil who sleeps fewer hours will fail
questions.explanation: A survey showing association cannot by itself isolate sleep from other possible influences.
questions.hint: Ask whether the study controlled other explanations.

questions.stem: A pupil compares temperature and catalase activity but tests only 10°C and 50°C. Which improvement would best help identify an optimum in between?
options: Add more temperatures between 10 and 50°C
Change enzyme source at each temperature
Use only the 50°C result
Remove the temperature labels from the graph
questions.explanation: Using more values within the tested range could reveal where the peak occurs.
questions.hint: Look for a change that fills a gap in the independent variable values.

questions.stem: A study of daisies uses one quadrat at every distance. Which improvement specifically helps judge consistency?
options: Reduce the size of the quadrat for distant locations
Use repeated quadrats at each distance and compare counts
Change the plant species for each quadrat
Record the results without the distances
questions.explanation: Repeated samples at each distance allow the spread and reliability of counts to be assessed.
questions.hint: Look for repeats under comparable conditions.

questions.stem: A lamp-distance experiment moves the lamp but the water temperature rises near the lamp. Which specific change improves validity?
options: Use a different species of pondweed at every distance
Count only the last minute at the closest distance
Increase water temperature as lamp distance increases
Use an appropriate heat barrier or thermostatically control water temperature
questions.explanation: The improvement reduces a temperature difference that might otherwise affect bubble production.
questions.hint: What unwanted variable is changing alongside distance?

questions.stem: Which is the most useful evaluation of a study with one reading at each pH?
options: It was a nice experiment
It should be better next time
Repeat measurements at every pH so the consistency of the results can be assessed
Everything should be controlled somehow
questions.explanation: A useful evaluation identifies a limitation and a specific, linked improvement.
questions.hint: Look for a practical change and a clear scientific reason.

questions.stem: A student counts gas bubbles to estimate pondweed photosynthesis. Which limitation is scientifically relevant?
options: Bubbles may differ in size, so number of bubbles is not exactly the gas volume
All gas bubbles have equal volumes by definition
Counting bubbles is a direct measurement of sugar made
Lamp distance cannot be measured with a ruler
questions.explanation: Different-sized bubbles can contain different gas volumes; counting them is only a proxy for gas production.
questions.hint: Consider whether the counting method measures the intended quantity directly.

questions.stem: Pitfall traps are used in two habitats. Which improvement most directly addresses unequal sampling effort?
options: Use different trap types in each habitat
Keep trap number and time deployed the same in each habitat
Change bait in just one habitat
Only count large invertebrates in woodland
questions.explanation: Equal trap numbers and deployment times make the comparison more valid.
questions.hint: Make the sampling conditions alike.

questions.stem: A pupil says “use better equipment” to improve a transpiration experiment. Which suggested change is more useful?
options: Use expensive equipment
Move plants to a different classroom each time
Use more worksheets
Use the same calibrated balance to measure mass change at each time point
questions.explanation: The revised suggestion identifies an actual measuring method that could increase consistency.
questions.hint: An evaluation should state what to change, not just that it should be “better”.

questions.stem: A study reports a strong growth effect but no control was used. What is an appropriate evaluation?
options: The effect must be caused by the treatment
A graph alone fixes the missing control
Include an untreated control to show the difference compared with no treatment
Repeating the conclusion makes it more valid
questions.explanation: An untreated control gives a baseline against which the observed treatment effect can be judged.
questions.hint: Think about what comparison is missing.

questions.stem: Which equipment is most appropriate for estimating daisy abundance in grassland?
options: A quadrat
A pitfall trap
A respirometer
A microscope slide
questions.explanation: A quadrat samples plants within a known area, allowing counts or percentage cover to be estimated.
questions.hint: Plants stay in place, so choose equipment that defines a sample area.

questions.stem: Which technique could be used to sample ground-dwelling invertebrates such as beetles?
options: Colorimetry
A potometer
A centrifuge
A pitfall trap
questions.explanation: Pitfall traps collect invertebrates moving over the soil surface.
questions.hint: Think about organisms moving along the ground.

questions.stem: A student wants to sample the distribution of plants from the bottom to the top of a slope. Which method is most appropriate?
options: Place every quadrat at the bottom
Use a transect line with samples at measured intervals
Measure only one plant in a classroom
Collect soil without noting distance
questions.explanation: A transect records change along an environmental gradient using known positions.
questions.hint: Which method follows a line across changing conditions?

questions.stem: To estimate average daisy abundance in a large, fairly uniform grass field, why might quadrats be placed at randomly selected positions?
options: To ensure every quadrat contains daisies
To guarantee a particular conclusion
To reduce selection bias in sampling locations
To find only the highest daisy counts
questions.explanation: Random positioning reduces the risk that a sampler selects convenient or unusually dense patches.
questions.hint: Try to avoid choosing places because of their expected result.

questions.stem: Which is an abiotic factor that could be measured during fieldwork?
options: Number of predators
Number of woodlice
Number of grass species
Soil pH
questions.explanation: Soil pH is a non-living environmental condition; the other options involve living organisms.
questions.hint: Abiotic means a non-living condition.

questions.stem: Five equal-sized quadrats are placed 1–5 m from a path. What must be recorded to study a distribution pattern?
options: Distance from the path and number of daisies per quadrat
Only the names of other flowers
Only the total number of pupils helping
Only the weather forecast
questions.explanation: You need location along the transect and a measurement of abundance to relate distribution to distance.
questions.hint: Record both position and biological observation.

questions.stem: A class sets pitfall traps to sample invertebrates. Which approach best reflects responsible sampling?
options: Leave traps open indefinitely without checking
Follow school guidance, minimise harm and check traps appropriately
Add harmful chemicals to ensure more specimens
Keep protected animals without permission
questions.explanation: Fieldwork should be supervised, risk assessed and conducted to minimise unnecessary harm to organisms.
questions.hint: Safety and welfare matter as well as data quality.

questions.stem: A 1 m² quadrat contains eight daisies. How should the observation be reported?
options: Eight daisies per kilogram
Eight daisies per minute
Eight daisies per square metre in the sampled quadrat
Eight daisies in the entire habitat
questions.explanation: The quadrat represents a known area; one sample should not be described as the total for the whole habitat.
questions.hint: State the measured sample area and avoid extrapolating from one sample.

questions.stem: Water produced a 0 mm clear zone, extract A 6 mm and extract B 14 mm. What is supported by the data?
options: Extract B produced the largest clear zone in this test
Extract B is safe for use as a medicine in humans
Extract A kills all forms of bacteria
The experiment proves extract B will work in every habitat
questions.explanation: The result supports a comparison of clear-zone diameters in this bacterial test, not clinical safety or universal effectiveness.
questions.hint: Stay close to what was measured.

questions.stem: A survey of only six pupils finds an association between breakfast and concentration. What limitation matters?
options: The sample proves the same result in all UK schools
The small sample may not represent the wider pupil population
All surveys must be experimental to record results
There is no possible relationship between food and concentration
questions.explanation: A small sample may be unrepresentative, so generalising to a much larger population is uncertain.
questions.hint: Consider whether the participants represent everyone being discussed.

questions.stem: Plant height falls at the highest fertiliser amount. Which claim is *not* established by height results alone?
options: Mean height differed between fertiliser amounts
Height was 11 cm at 8 g
The exact cellular mechanism causing the drop in height has been identified
Mean height was greater at 4 g than at 0 g
questions.explanation: Height data describe the pattern but do not identify which internal biological mechanism caused it.
questions.hint: Distinguish an observed pattern from its untested biological cause.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest way to support a conclusion about plant growth?
options: State that everyone knows the answer
Use a confident tone instead of measurements
Ignore results from other sources
Link the claim to relevant measurements and acknowledge any conflicting data
questions.explanation: Conclusions should be grounded in evidence, including limitations and differences rather than selective reporting.
questions.hint: Look for evidence rather than authority or confidence.

questions.stem: A pupil finds faster germination in light, while a published study reports no difference for the same species. What should the pupil do?
options: Report the difference and consider methods and conditions that could explain it
Delete the published study
Claim the published study must be dishonest
Change the pupil’s results to match the published data
questions.explanation: Responsible analysis discusses similarities and differences and possible explanations; it does not change or ignore evidence.
questions.hint: Scientists compare all available evidence, even when results disagree.

questions.stem: Pondweed bubble count decreases across distances from 10 to 40 cm. Which prediction is most reasonable if tested at 30 cm?
options: More than 100 bubbles per minute
About 9 bubbles per minute
Zero bubbles at every distance
Exactly 28 bubbles per minute
questions.explanation: The displayed value at 30 cm is 9 bubbles per minute, so this is a directly grounded expectation.
questions.hint: Locate 30 cm on the horizontal axis first.

questions.stem: A student tests an extract against one bacterial species and finds a clear zone. What is a limitation of claiming it works against all bacteria?
options: There was a measurable clear zone
A ruler was used for the measurement
Only one species was tested, so the conclusion cannot be generalised to all bacteria
The control disc had no extract
questions.explanation: Results from one species cannot establish the same effect across all species without additional testing.
questions.hint: Consider the breadth of organisms actually investigated.
